old_title: Iran war live: Trump aides 'urgently trying to stop war escalating' despite strikes
new_title: Iran war live: Trump labels strikes a 'love tap' in bizarre rant after fresh bombings
old_text:
Donald Trump's top White House aides are urgently pushing to prevent the Iran war from escalating, after the US ramped up the intensity of its attacks on Wednesday.
The aides want to prevent the war escalating before November's midterm elections to hinder Republican electoral losses, four sources told the Reuters news agency.
Officials will consider once again ramping up military action after the vote in November, but a return to the full-scale conflict is not a fiven, they said.
"We are keeping the pressure on Iran," one White House official said. "But November is a priority."
It comes after Iran vowed to respond with "crushing and devastating blows" after US strikes killed five people attending a wedding party in Iran.
Iranian state media reported explosions across southern coastal areas, including Bandar Abbas and Qeshm Island. Tehran also said US strikes hit civilian sites in Hormozgan province and a civilian airport in Kerman province.
One of the strikes hit a home in Kuhestak where a wedding ceremony was taking place, killing five people, including a child, and wounding at least 68 others, according to Hormozgan provincial officials.
Centcom said it concluded its latest barrage against Iranian military targets on Tuesday night.
Pictured: Centcom shares footage of Iranian military target before strike
Trump's aides push to prevent Iran war from escalating - Reuters
Senior aides to Donald Trump are pushing to prevent the Iran war from escalating, after the US ramped up the intensity of its attacks on Wednesday.
The aides want to prevent the war escalating before November's midterm elections to hinder Republican electoral losses, four sources told the Reuters news agency.
Officials will consider once again ramping up military action after the vote in November, but a return to the full-scale conflict is not a fiven, they said.
They said that for now, the administration is focused on tightening the economic pressure on Iran in an effort to extract concessions in any future negotiation that months of military action failed to secure.
"We are keeping the pressure on Iran," one White House official said. "But November is a priority."
Keeping the war mostly contained until then would help prevent the unpopular conflict from dominating the news as Trump's Republicans campaign to defend thin majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, said the sources, three of whom are White House officials.
Exhausted and demoralised? How US sailors are really coping after six months at sea
While President Trump and his self-styled secretary of state for "War", Pete Hegseth, dismissed it as 'fake news', by all accounts, life for the 5,000 men and women on board the USS Abraham Lincoln had become a living nightmare after more than 260 days at sea without respite.
The nuclear-powered warship left San Diego in November and has, until recently, been stationed in the Middle East to support the U.S. war against Iran. While the Lincoln left the Middle East on August 22 on its way home, with a planned Thailand stop, she has spent a record amount of time at sea without a port visit. Stories abound about poor food, bad hygiene, blocked toilets, intermittent showers, plummeting morale and shredded mental health. Reports in the Military Times and the Stars and Stripes claimed that sailors even tried to jump overboard as the deployment kept going.
Chris Terrill reports:
Oil tankers hit sea mines while transiting Strait of Hormuz, says Tehran
Two oil tankers hit sea mines and were disabled while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday.
In a statement shared by state media, the guards said the tankers had been forced to disembark their crews and were placed in the hands of US operatives to pass through what it called an "illegal route" in the strategic waterway.
It came despite earlier warnings from the Guards' navy about the dangers of crossing the mined passage, the statement added.
Two killed in security incident in Strait of Hormuz, says Saudi shipping company
Two Filipino seafarers have been killed in a security incident in the Strait of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia's national shipping company, Bahri, said on Wednesday.
The incident involved the company's vessel "SIDR" while it was transiting the Strait of Hormuz on August 31, it said.
Bahri did not provide further details - we'll bring you more on this incident as we get it.

Pakistan confident US and Iran will 'return to the table'
Pakistan is working with the US and Iran to end their conflict and believes they will soon "return to the table for dialogue".
Foreign ministry spokesperson Tahir Andrabi made the comments at a regular media briefing on Wednesday.
The visit last month of Pakistan's Chief of Defence Forces Asim Munir to Tehran created "considerable momentum" on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz, he said.
Moscow helping Iran produce supersonic cruise missiles - report
Iran is secretly developing advanced supersonic cruise missiles with the help of Russia, according to a report.
The C430L programme, which has spanned several years since 2023, has seen Moscow's top missile specialists helping produce the weapons that would significantly strengthen Tehran's military, with the prospect of total peace with the US currently looking bleak.
It was reported by the Financial Times, which dubbed the programme as one of the most "significant known transfers of strategic military technology from Moscow to Tehran".
Moscow is assisting Tehran in developing a ramjet propulsion system, which would enable cruise missiles to fly much faster than the speed of sound, according to military patents and leaked Russian correspondence, the FT reported.
Iranian missile expert Fabian Hinz, an analyst at Conflict Armament Research, told the outlet: "This is the transfer of a highly strategically sensitive military technology from Russia that the Iranians have wanted to acquire for decades.
"A programme like this would require political clearance from the very top in Russia."
Trump insists US has 'almost total control' of Hormuz - recap
Donald Trump has insisted that the US has "almost total control" of the Strait of Hormuz.
"I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing", the US president said of Iran on Truth Social earlier Wednesday morning. "They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?"
Kuwait races to contain fire at a residential complex in capital after drone strike
Firefighters in Kuwait rushed to contain a blaze at a residential complex in the capital after it was struck by an Iranian drone.
Public Fire Force spokesperson Brigadier General Mohammed Al-Gharib said on Wednesday, that the fire had been doused and blamed "a hostile drone" from Iran for the attack.
new_text:
Donald Trump has labelled Iran's strikes on US targets as a "love tap" after US forces had hit the country "very hard" in yet another bizarre rant.
Iranians, Europeans, and others in the region fear a return of the conflict in earnest after the biggest exchange of fire between Tehran and Washington since July took place on Wednesday.
"It was a very heavy attack last night, and we're prepared to do another one anytime we want," Trump said on Wednesday according to Fox News.
"We have technology that's incredible. Nobody has technology like we have. So, we hit them hard last night, very hard. They gave a little love tap, but we hit them very hard."
It comes amid fears Trump is planning to extend Washington's war on Iran, after The Wall Street Journal reported that the Pentagon was extending the presence of troops in the Middle East into next year.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is quietly stretching the presence of troops in the region as part of an strategy to leave Trump with open-ended options in the war, sources told the outlet.
Trump said the US is prepared to launch another attack at "any time", but added that a renewed campaign would not last "too long".
Oil edges down as investors weigh uncertainty
Oil prices edged lower on Thursday as investors weighed the uncertainty of renewed military strikes between the US and Iran that risk disrupting supplies from the Middle East.
Brent crude futures fell 43 cents, or 0.45 per cent, to $95.2 a barrel at 0029 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down 24 cents, or 0.26 per cent, at $90.77.
Brent and WTI swung between gains of as much as $2 a barrel and losses of $1 a barrel during the previous trading session. The session highs for both benchmarks were the highest since 24 July.
Trump under pressure to avoid Iran escalation ahead of midterms
Donald Trump is under pressure to avoid further escalation after the US launched its largest wave of strikes on Iran in weeks, as the military faces mounting strain and the November midterm elections approach.
Trump on Wednesday dismissed concerns that the war could hurt Republican candidates, saying he believed his party supported his efforts to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
But the president's approval rating has fallen to a record-low 33 per cent, while two-thirds of Americans disapprove of his handling of the war. Oil prices also climbed above $90 a barrel on Wednesday.
"I don't think it will be very much longer," Trump said when asked how many more Iranian targets the US could strike, as the conflict passed the six-month mark.
The comments came as Reuters reported that the White House was seeking to avoid a major escalation against Iran until after the 3 November election.
The latest fighting erupted after a month of relative calm. US forces carried out about 100 strikes against Iranian targets on Tuesday, saying they were retaliation for maritime threats near the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian state media reported that a US strike hit a home in southern Iran during a wedding celebration, killing two women and two children and injuring 60 others.
Trump floats renaming Strait of Hormuz as 'Trump Strait' - ICYMI
President Donald Trump suggested on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz should be renamed after him, claiming the key waterway is now under US control.
"Now that we have it under USA control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT???" Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
The waterway has become a flashpoint in the renewed conflict between the US and Iran. The latest escalation began after US forces struck what an American military spokesperson said were Iranian Revolutionary Guard forces preparing to lay more sea mines in the strait.
Trump last month also vowed to declare the Strait of Hormuz US territory.

USS Abraham Lincoln sailors finally reach steady land - and are warned against engaging in Thailand's sex tourism
The USS Abraham Lincoln has docked after nearly nine months at sea, allowing sailors to finally hit the town in Pattaya, known as Thailand's "Sin City."
These roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines have been on the aircraft carrier since it left its home port of San Diego on November 21. While the ship briefly docked in Guam and Oman, American service members have spent virtually all of their time on the ship, reportedly facing food shortages and mental health challenges as their deployment dragged out amid the ongoing Iran war.
A trip to Pattaya will be a much-needed reprieve for sailors, where they can enjoy the seaside resort's beaches and nightlife.
"He's so excited to get on land, he's never been outside of the United States before. He wants to eat pizza or McDonald's. I'm so happy for him," the mother of one of the sailors on the USS Lincoln told MS NOW.
Pattaya has been rebranded as a more family-friendly destination in recent years following a history of sex tourism. The USS Lincoln's commanding officer warned service members against engaging in prostitution, a person familiar with the matter told MS NOW.
Prostitution is technically illegal in Thailand, but the law is rarely enforced. Paying for sex is also a punishable offense in the U.S. armed forces.
During the Vietnam War, American service members flocked to Pattaya, once a quiet fishing village, "and it turned into a raunchy seaside playground," Elizabeth Becker wrote in "Overbooked: The Exploding Business of Travel and Tourism," according to the Associated Press.
Iran's rial drops to new low of 2.2 million to the dollar, tracking websites show
Iran's currency has dropped to a record low of more than 2.2 million rials per U.S. dollar, two websites tracking the free market rate showed on Wednesday, amid renewed military strikes.
The rial has dropped about 10 per cent in the past week. The troubled currency has lost about half of its value in a year of tightening U.S. sanctions and U.S. and Israeli attacks that began in February.
Full report: Russia is secretly helping Iran to develop supersonic cruise missiles, says report
Russia has been helping Iran to develop supersonic cruise missiles in secret for years, including through the US-Iran war, according to a report.
Moscow has enlisted some of its most experienced specialists to help Iran to develop a new class of missile capable of threatening US aircraft carriers and warships stationed in the Middle East, according to an investigation by the Financial Times.
The programme's central objective was to help Iran to develop a special 'ramjet' propulsion system that would allow its cruise missiles to fly at several times the speed of sound, the report said.
Fabian Hinz, an expert on Iranian missiles, framed the programme as a major transfer of sensitive technology from Moscow that Tehran had been after for decades and would require authorisation "from the very top".
Senior foreign reporter James Reynolds writes:
Bab el-Mandeb Strait sees highest number of vessels since 24 August
The Bab el-Mandeb strait, the waterway between Yemen and the horn of Africa, has seen the highest number of vessels transiting since 24 August.
A total of 31 commodity vessels crossed that waterway on Wednesday, above the 10-day average of 25 vessels, Kpler data showed.
On Tuesday, 17 vessels transited the waterway, the data showed.
As we reported earlier, six commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, down from 11 a day earlier and well below the 10-day average of about 13, the Kpler data showed according to Reuters news agency.
Trump discusses Iran war with UAE president
Donald Trump has been on the phone with UAE president Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, UAE state news agency WAM said on Thursday.
The pair discussed the ongoing developments in the Iran war, and touched on further bilateral cooperation between the two.
We'll bring you any further lines from the call as they come in.
